country.name: Poland
country.tagline: A medieval wine country, then Germany's northernmost Sekt town, now one of Europe's fastest-growing young vineyards.

stats.note: About 500 ha in 2011 and 433 vineyards in 2017 (Wikipedia de); the area has grown since but no reliable current figure was found.

country.overview:
Wine is part of Polish history from the start. Grape seeds found on Wawel hill in Kraków suggest vines around the year 1000, a papal bull of 1136 mentions vineyards near Płock and Włocławek, and Cistercian monks at Paradyż (Paradies) were making wine near Zielona Góra by 1250. In the fourteenth century there were vineyards from Silesia and Greater Poland to Toruń, Sandomierz and Kraków. The Little Ice Age and cheap Hungarian wine, especially Tokaji, which Polish nobles adored, pushed most of them out.

The great exception was Zielona Góra (German Grünberg) in Lower Silesia, then part of Prussia. Its slopes held thousands of small vineyards, and in 1826 the firm Häusler, Förster und Grempler began making sparkling wine by the Champagne method there, among the first in Germany; the town's harvest festival has been held since 1852. After 1945 the German population was expelled, and Silesian viticulture almost vanished; the communist state favoured fruit wines. The Barossa Valley's Henschke and Lehmann families trace their roots to the region.

The revival began with hobby growers and a 2008 wine law that made commercial sale practical. Hundreds of small vineyards now grow fungus-resistant varieties such as Solaris, Johanniter, Regent and Rondo, along with Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Seyval Blanc. Leading areas are Lubuskie around Zielona Góra, Lower Silesia, Małopolska around Kraków (Srebrna Góra, 28 ha, in the city), the Vistula valley around Sandomierz and Kazimierz Dolny, Podkarpacie near Jasło, and even West Pomerania, where Winnica Turnau is one of the country's largest estates. Poland has no EU-registered wine PDO in the dataset used here.

history.title: Vines on Wawel hill
history.text: Archaeobotanical finds suggest grapes were grown on Wawel hill in Kraków around the year 1000.

history.title: Cistercians and Grünberg
history.text: Monks of the Cistercian abbey of Paradyż made wine by 1250, and vineyards around Zielona Góra are recorded from 1314.

history.title: Grünberg sparkling wine and the Winobranie
history.text: Häusler, Förster und Grempler began traditional-method sparkling wine in Grünberg in 1826; the town's annual wine festival dates from 1852.

history.title: Expulsion and decline
history.text: With the expulsion of the German population of Silesia, its viticulture almost disappeared; the communist economy turned to fruit wine.

history.title: A modern wine law
history.text: A wine law adopted in 2008 (and later amended) let small producers sell wine commercially, triggering rapid growth.

country.classification: Poland lies in EU wine zone A. Growers may sell wine with a Polish origin and varietal and vintage labelling; the country has defined grape-growing areas, but no wine PDO appears in the EU dataset used for this atlas (Candiago et al. 2022). Check eAmbrosia for any newer registrations.
country.climate_soils: Cool continental with cold winters and warm summers; the south and west (Lower Silesia, Lubuskie, Małopolska, Podkarpacie) are warmest. Soils include loess (Sandomierz, Kazimierz), limestone (Kraków), glacial sands and clays (Lubuskie, Pomerania) and flysch (Podkarpacie).

regions.name: Lubuskie (Zielona Góra)
regions.summary: Zielona Góra, the 'city of wine', had thousands of vineyards at its peak and made Prussian sparkling wine from 1826. Today the Lubuskie wine route links dozens of new vineyards, including the large Zabór estate (about 35 ha), and the Palm House on Wine Hill and the September Winobranie festival keep the tradition alive.
regions.history: Vineyards from at least 1314 and a Prussian sparkling-wine industry from 1826 made Grünberg the northernmost notable wine town of its time.
regions.terroir: Glacial sands and clays on gentle hills; cool continental climate.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds

regions.name: Dolny Śląsk (Lower Silesia)
regions.tagline: Young vineyards in the warm south-west.
regions.summary: Lower Silesia around Wrocław, Trzebnica and the Sudeten foothills has some of Poland's oldest modern vineyards, such as Winnica Jaworek, and a warm, sheltered climate.
regions.history: Cistercians and Silesian towns grew vines in the Middle Ages; Trzebnica's hills were among the first replanted after 1990.
regions.terroir: Loess and clay in the Trzebnica hills, varied soils in the Sudeten foothills; one of Poland's warmest areas.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds

regions.name: Małopolska
regions.summary: Małopolska has medieval roots on Wawel hill and a modern cluster of vineyards on Jurassic limestone around Kraków, led by Srebrna Góra (about 28 ha) below the Camaldolese monastery at Bielany, and Winnica Garlicki.
regions.history: Grape seeds on Wawel suggest vines around 1000; monasteries and the royal court in Kraków kept vineyards in the Middle Ages.
regions.terroir: Jurassic limestone and loess around Kraków.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds

regions.name: Vistula Valley (Sandomierz and Kazimierz)
regions.summary: The Vistula valley around Sandomierz and Kazimierz Dolny has loess hills with a long wine history; Winnica Płochockich near Sandomierz is a well-known estate.
regions.history: Sandomierz had medieval vineyards on its loess hills, and the area was among the first in modern Poland to replant.
regions.terroir: Deep loess on hills above the Vistula; warm, sunny summers.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds

regions.name: Podkarpacie
regions.summary: Podkarpacie in the south-east, around Jasło, Krosno and Przemyśl, revived its vineyards from the 1980s and hosts an annual wine festival in Jasło.
regions.history: Krosno and Przemyśl had medieval vineyards and traded in Hungarian wine; the modern revival began in the 1980s.
regions.terroir: Carpathian flysch, clay and loess in the foothills.
regions.grapes: Solaris, Johanniter, Regent, Rondo, Riesling, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Seyval Blanc
regions.styles: Dry whites, sparkling, rosé, light reds

sites.name: Palm House on Wine Hill, Zielona Góra
sites.text: A glass palm house on Zielona Góra's Wine Hill, surrounded by a small vineyard, symbol of the city's wine tradition and centre of the Winobranie festival held since 1852.

sites.name: Winnica Srebrna Góra
sites.text: A vineyard on limestone slopes below the Camaldolese monastery at Bielany in Kraków, one of Poland's largest.

sites.name: Winnica Turnau
sites.text: A large vineyard at Baniewice in West Pomerania, near the German border, one of Poland's most successful modern wineries.

sites.name: Winnica Płochockich
sites.text: A family vineyard and guest house at Przyłogi near Sandomierz in the Vistula valley.

sites.name: Winnica Jasło
sites.text: A vineyard at Ulaszowice near Jasło, the centre of Podkarpacie's wine revival.
